::: {.notes}
**Say:** The strongest single source so far is not a blazar but NGC 1068 — a nearby galaxy whose bright core is hidden by dust. Similar X-ray-bright galaxies seem to shine in neutrinos too.

The Hubble image is an observation, not an image of a resolved neutrino engine.
The current northern-track analysis covers 13.1 years. NGC 1068 has a best-fit
102 signal events and spectral index 3.4±0.2. Its local significance is 5.0
sigma; the 110-source catalogue gives 4.0 sigma after trials, while the
northern-sky scan gives 1.4 sigma after sky trials. The 4.2-sigma catalogue
value belongs to the 2022 result, not this updated analysis.

Allow about three minutes: the directional excess, Photons and neutrinos,
then the X-ray population. The current all-flavour spectral comparison is
optional.

The photon comparison redraws the 2022 figure from its vector artwork, with a
muon-neutrino plus antineutrino fit, not the 2026 all-flavour spectrum. Its blue
band is 95% confidence within 1.5–15 TeV, the well-constrained range of that
analysis. Grey points are archival photon measurements; orange marks the
4FGL-DR2 Fermi points and the Fermi and MAGIC upper limits (arrows). The violet
band and violet curve are the two theoretical core models (Inoue et al. band,
Murase et al. curve), shortened to "core models" in the legend.
Compare observed high-energy photons with the neutrino component under a hadronic
production hypothesis, then recall internal absorption and reprocessing. Dust
obscuration of a Seyfert nucleus does not alone establish gamma-gamma opacity
or a neutrino production site. No direct spatial localization of the corona
is claimed.

The spectral figure retains its source/all-flavour and diffuse-flux conventions.
Bands are fitted uncertainties, not measurements of the emission location.
The excess at TeV energies and weak high-energy gamma-ray emission motivate
opaque-core/corona models. The production region has not been spatially resolved.

The separate X-ray catalogue contains 47 sources and excludes NGC 1068.
Its most significant ensemble contains 11 sources and gives 3.3 sigma after
the population trials. The ensemble includes individually weak directions;
it is not a catalogue of eleven discoveries. A complementary southern
starting-track analysis of 14 Seyferts reports 3.0-sigma stacking evidence.
These sample definitions and significances cannot be added as independent
Gaussian measurements without accounting for their analyses and overlaps.

[2022 photon comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09972v1);
[Northern AGN analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13403);
[Southern Seyfert analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10208);
[NGC 1068 models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03381).
:::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** Blazars — galaxies whose jets point straight at us — are the second suspect: a famous alert in 2017, a Baikal neutrino from the same direction in 2021, both at the start of radio flares, and radio astronomers finding that neutrinos like the brightest radio jets.

Allow about three minutes: 2017 alert, GVD 2021, Radio flares and Radio
blazars. The tabs 2014–15 flare and Reprocessed are reserve.

2017 alert: IceCube-170922A triggered the electromagnetic follow-up. The movie
shows the recorded DOM signals and reconstructed muon track, not simulated photon
trajectories. The most probable parent energy is about 290 TeV under the source
paper's spectral assumption, not a calorimetric measurement. The approximately
3-sigma association concerns the neutrino and the flaring blazar.

GVD 2021: GVD210418CA, the highest-energy upward-going GVD cascade at the
time, eight clusters operating. Shower energy 224 TeV; the paper's ±75 TeV is a
three-sigma interval. The 90% directional containment radius is 6.2 degrees and
contains TXS 0506+056. These radii (50% 3.4°, 90% 6.2°) are those of the 2023
analysis and its figure; Table 1 of the 2025 Galactic paper lists r90 = 5.8° for
the same cascade from a later reconstruction, so the two numbers differ. Atmospheric-background probability 0.0033 for the event's
energy, hits and direction; signalness 97.1% for an E^-2.46 astrophysical
spectrum. The chance that one such cascade falls this close to TXS is below 0.8%.
These are not posterior probabilities that TXS produced it; a single event
cannot establish the origin. The same cascade is one of the eight GVD events
of the Galactic analysis.

Radio flares: Fermi-LAT gamma rays (white) and RATAN-600 11 GHz radio (orange
diamonds; thick line the fitted sum, thin dotted lines the three flares and the
baseline; grey line the median gamma-ray flux), digitized from the original. IceCube-170922A and GVD210418CA both arrived
near the start of large radio flares; the 2014–15 excess had no gamma-ray flare.
The authors stress that an a posteriori chance probability is hard to define.

Radio blazars: 56 IceCube events above 200 TeV and a complete
VLBI-flux-limited AGN sample at 8 GHz. AGN inside the error regions (enlarged
by 0.5 degrees for systematics) have stronger parsec-scale cores; post-trial
chance probability p = 2e-3 (0.2%). Four strongest associations: 3C 279,
NRAO 530, PKS 1741−038, PKS 2145+067. The 2021 ICRC update adds lower-energy
IceCube sky-map information and quotes a joint chance probability 4e-5 (4.1
sigma). RATAN-600 monitoring shows radio flares near neutrino arrival times,
most clearly PKS 1502+106. Independent tests differ: an analysis of the IceCube
ten-year release and the IceCube real-time alert search with radio-bright AGN
(arXiv:2304.12675) found no significant correlation. The slide states this
explicitly: evidence under debate, not an established population. IceCube
reports that adding more event information and more data makes the result
compatible with background.

Reserve, archival flare: separate 2014–2015 dataset; Gaussian time-profile
analysis found 13±5 signal events in a roughly 110-day flare, 3.5 sigma after
time-search trials. Marker height is an event weight, not a count or light curve.
Reserve, updated reconstruction: the 2023 reprocessing changes directions,
uncertainties, classifications and likelihood weights; two cascade-like events
are excluded. The pre-trial p-value becomes 1e-3 instead of 7e-5, and the fitted
flux is roughly halved. These p-values exclude the seasons/livetime trial factor
and are not comparable to the historical trial-corrected 3.5 sigma.

[2017 association](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.08816);
[Archival flare](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.08794);
[Updated reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.14559);
[Baikal-GVD candidate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.13686v1);
[Plavin et al., ApJ 894, 101 (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00930v3);
[Plavin et al., ICRC 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09053);
[IceCube radio-AGN alert search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.12675).
:::

$$E_\mu=120^{+110}_{-60}\,\mathrm{PeV}$$

:::

::: {.media-caption}
Drawn from the numbers in the text of [KM3NeT, Nature (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08543-1) · Their Fig. 2 (CC BY-NC-ND) is kept unmodified for questions
:::

::::::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** In 2023 KM3NeT, still a fraction of its final size, recorded the most energetic neutrino ever seen — hundreds of PeV. Where it came from is still open.

Allow about 90 seconds: The event, then From light to energy.
ARCA had 21 detection units when the event occurred, not its current installed
configuration. The movie shows recorded PMT signals and a reconstructed track;
its cone is an artistic guide, not measured photon trajectories. The tab's
diagram is drawn from the published numbers only (assets/km3-energy); the
Nature Fig. 2 itself (simulated triggered-PMT distributions for 10, 100 and
1000 PeV muons) is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and is kept unmodified as
media/source-results/km3-energy-calibration.png for questions. The event triggered 3672 PMTs, about
35% of active PMTs, allowing comparison with simulations of matched muon
direction and position. Optical-property and detection-efficiency uncertainties
enter the inference. The muon-energy 90% confidence interval is 35–380 PeV.

The parent-neutrino distribution is conditional on the inferred muon and an
E^-2 incident spectrum. Median 220 PeV; central 68% range 110–790 PeV, central
90% range 72 PeV–2.6 EeV. It is not a direct neutrino calorimetric measurement.
The reconstructed direction is RA 94.3 degrees, declination −7.8 degrees;
the published 68% directional containment radius is 1.5 degrees. This is the
2025 analysis, not a claim of a later positional recalibration.

An astrophysical accelerator and a cosmogenic neutrino produced during
ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray propagation are alternative interpretations.
No counterpart is established. Diffuse-flux comparisons with IceCube depend
on assumed spectrum, sky distribution and exposure, rather than implying an
unconditional contradiction between detectors.

[KM3NeT observation](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08543-1);
[Global flux analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08173).
:::

:::

### Comparison with ANTARES

![](media/source-results/baikal-antares-limits-dark.svg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-max-height: 560px;" fig-alt="Redrawn comparison of Baikal-GVD and ANTARES 90% point-source limits for E^-2 and E^-2.5 spectra, with the declination axis of the original. This compares selected analysis samples, not equal-volume instruments."}

:::

::::::

::: {.notes}
**Say:** Baikal-GVD now looks for individual sources with muon tracks. No source stands out yet; the detector grows every year, and so does its reach.

Spend about one minute on Source limits. The spectral-assumption and ANTARES
comparisons are reserve material.
This first track-based GVD catalogue search uses 988 upward-going single-cluster
events from April 2019 to March 2024, about 30 cluster-years and 1.5 km3-years.
Typical angular resolution is about 0.5 degrees. No catalogue excess remains
significant after trials. The figure's 2019–2023 label refers to seasons.

The first graph reproduces the 92 published Table 1 values for E^-2 sources,
with the original gamma=2 normalization multiplied by 1e-8. For that spectrum,
the numerical normalization at 1 GeV equals E^2 Phi in GeV cm^-2 s^-1.
No fitted sensitivity curve or recomputed confidence interval is added.
The Spectral assumptions tab redraws figure 2 with all three spectra: limits
are the Table 1 values (column scales 1e-8, 1e-6, 1e-3 confirmed against the
plotted markers), the sensitivity curves are read from the vector artwork. Symbols are source limits; solid curves are median expected 90%-confidence
upper limits under the background-only hypothesis. The spectral index is an
assumption, not a measured property of each source. The normalization refers
to nu_mu+anti-nu_mu before Earth attenuation. Efficiency systematic uncertainty
is not included in these quoted limits. Exposure and event selections differ
from IceCube and ANTARES; absence of a significant GVD source excess does not
contradict the higher-exposure IceCube NGC 1068 result.

The comparison tab redraws figure 3: ANTARES 15-year limit markers read from
the vector artwork, GVD limits from Table 1, the same spectral assumptions. A sensitivity is not an observed limit
and a discovery potential is another statistical quantity.

[Baikal-GVD source search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21261v2).
:::
